title: Love Is as Strong as Death
summary: The woman wishes she could show her love openly, repeats the charge not to awaken love until its time, and then speaks the book's great statement: set me as a seal on your heart, for love is as strong as death, and many waters cannot quench it. The brothers remember a little sister, the woman declares herself a wall, contrasts Solomon's vast vineyard with her own freely given one, and the book ends with her calling her beloved to come away.
story: Chapter 7 reached the height of the lovers' delight in each other, with the woman inviting her beloved to the vineyards. Chapter 8 draws the book to a close, gathering its threads rather than tying them neatly. The refrain to the daughters of Jerusalem appears a third and final time (verse 4), the question “Who is this coming up from the wilderness” returns from 3:6, the brothers who were angry with her in 1:6 reappear, and Solomon, whose name opened the book, appears again in the vineyard parable. At the center stands verses 6 and 7, the only passage in the Song that steps back from the lovers to say what love itself is. The book then ends not with a wedding scene or a conclusion but with a call to come away, leaving the reader with love still in motion.
historical:
Nothing in the chapter can be dated to a particular event. Baal-hamon (verse 11), the site of Solomon's vineyard, is not known from any other source, and its name, which means something like owner of a multitude or lord of wealth, may be chosen for its meaning as much as its location. The thousand shekels of silver the tenants pay is a large sum; Isaiah 7:23 uses the same figure for a vineyard of a thousand vines, which suggests it was a conventional value for a large and productive vineyard. Solomon was famous for his wealth and his many wives (1 Kings 10 and 11), and his appearance here as a landowner with tenants fits that memory.

The poem's date and authorship remain debated, with proposals ranging from Solomon's own reign in the tenth century BC to the Persian or Hellenistic periods, depending on how scholars weigh the heading in 1:1 and features of the Hebrew. What is certain is that copies of the Song were among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and that Jewish tradition preserves a debate about its status: the Mishnah records Rabbi Akiva (early second century AD) defending it as the holiest of the Writings.
cultural:
In the woman's world, public affection between unmarried people, or even between spouses, drew disapproval, while affection between siblings was acceptable. Her wish that her beloved were like a brother (verse 1) is a wish to be able to show her love without shame. Bringing him to her mother's house (verse 2; compare 3:4) points to the mother's role in the household and perhaps in arranging marriage.

A seal (verse 6) was a carved stone, either a small cylinder or a stamp, which a person wore on a cord around the neck or as a ring on the hand (compare Judah's seal and cord in Genesis 38:18). It marked ownership and identity and was one of a person's most precious possessions. To ask to be set as a seal on the heart and arm is to ask to belong to the beloved as closely as that. Sheol was the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, pictured as a place that never has enough. Mighty waters recall the chaotic sea that neighboring peoples feared as a hostile power. The brothers' talk of their little sister (verses 8-9) reflects the role brothers played in protecting a sister and negotiating her marriage: if she is a wall, chaste and firm, they will honor her; if she is a door, they will guard her.
literary: The chapter is a series of short scenes, again marked mostly by changes of speaker. The woman speaks (verses 1-3), the refrain is repeated (verse 4), the friends ask a question and she answers (verse 5), and then comes the climactic speech of verses 6 and 7, built in tight parallel lines: love and death, jealousy and Sheol, fire and water. The refrain in verse 4 is shorter than in 2:7 and 3:5; the oath by the gazelles and does has dropped away. Verses 8 to 12 are two small parables about walls and vineyards, the woman's body and her choice. The last two verses end the book with an open invitation that echoes 2:17, but where 2:17 names the mountains of Bether, 8:14 names the mountains of spices. The book does not conclude so much as fall silent while the lovers are still speaking.

outline.t: If only you were like a brother
His embrace and the last charge to the daughters of Jerusalem
The little sister and the wall

doctrines.note: Verses 6 and 7 describe love as exclusive, permanent, and beyond price, which is the Bible's picture of the marriage covenant. Love cannot be bought (verse 7), and it asks to be sealed. The refrain of verse 4 adds that love must be protected and not rushed.

God is never clearly named in the Song. The final syllable of the word for flame in verse 6 may be a short form of God's name (Yah), which would make this the book's only mention of him; others take it as a Hebrew way of saying mightiest. Either way, the book teaches about God by showing a love fierce and faithful enough to point beyond itself.

Many scholars place the Song near the Bible's wisdom books. The reflection in verses 6 and 7 reads like a proverb about love: its strength, its jealousy, and its refusal to be purchased. Wisdom here includes knowing the worth and the power of love.

words.note: Chotam, seal or signet. A seal was worn close to the body and used to sign and claim. The woman asks to be as close to her beloved as his seal and to mark him as hers. The same image appears in Haggai 2:23, where God says he will make Zerubbabel like a signet ring.

Qin'ah, jealousy or zeal. In English jealousy is usually a vice, but the Hebrew word can mean an intense, exclusive devotion that refuses to share its object. The Old Testament often uses it of God himself, who is jealous for his people. Here it describes love's fierce refusal to let go, as unrelenting as the grave.

Shalhevet, flame, in verse 6 in a longer form that ends with the syllable -yah. That ending may be a short form of God's name, making the phrase a flame of the LORD, or it may simply intensify the word (the fiercest blaze). Translations and scholars divide on this, and the ambiguity is itself suggestive.

Ahavah, love, used four times in this chapter. It is the ordinary Old Testament noun for love, used of friendship, of marriage, and of God's own love for Israel (Deuteronomy 7:8; Jeremiah 31:3). In the Song it names the power the whole book has been describing.

christ: The Song ends without mentioning God directly, but its closing claim that love is as strong as death reads differently in light of the whole Bible. The New Testament proclaims a love that is not only as strong as death but stronger: Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25), and death could not hold him. Paul's confidence that nothing, not death nor life, can separate us from the love of God in Christ (Romans 8:38-39) is a thematic echo of the Song's many waters that cannot quench love. Christians have also connected the seal of verse 6 with the New Testament's language of believers sealed with the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13). These are connections of theme, not predictions, and the chapter is first of all about human love. But faithful human love, sealed and costly, is one of the clearest pictures Scripture offers of the love God has shown in Christ.

hard.q: How can a book that never clearly mentions God belong in the Bible, and what are its readers supposed to learn from it?
hard.a: The Song's place in Scripture was questioned in antiquity, and Jewish tradition preserves the debate. It was defended and received partly because it was read as describing God's love for Israel, and Christians likewise read it for centuries as describing Christ and the church or the soul. Today many readers, including many committed Christians, read it first as love poetry and find its place in the canon justified on those terms: God made human love and desire, and a book celebrating them within faithful commitment belongs among his words just as Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, with their attention to ordinary life, do. Others hold that the allegorical or typological reading remains essential, noting that Scripture repeatedly uses marriage to describe God's covenant. These readings need not cancel each other. The book teaches the goodness and power of love between a man and a woman, and because that love was made to mirror God's own faithful love, it teaches something about him as well. Esther, the other book that does not clearly name God, shows that God can be present in Scripture without being named on every page.

questions: Verse 7 says love cannot be bought. What does that say about the ways people try to earn, buy, or manipulate love?
The brothers wonder whether their sister will be a wall or a door. What does it mean to guard love and not awaken it before its time?
Love is called as strong as death. Where have you seen love hold on through loss, and what does that suggest about God's love?
